Posterior 1/3 of tongue — general and taste sensation by glossopharyngeal nerve
Posterior-most part of tongue — general and taste sensation by vagus nerve

cloze.text: The tongue is formed by the first {{c1::four}} paired {{c2::pharyngeal}} arches.
cloze.extra: Did you know? Tongue prints are as unique as fingerprints.

cloze.text: The body (front) of the tongue develops from the {{c1::first}} paired pharyngeal arches; the base (back) develops from the {{c2::second, third, and fourth}} paired arches.
The lateral lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar form the {{c1::anterior 2/3}} of the tongue.
The {{c1::copula}} swellings form the base of the tongue.
The {{c1::sulcus terminalis}} is the area toward the back of the tongue where the body and the base of the tongue fuse together.
The {{c1::thyroid gland}} forms originally around the tongue and migrates down the neck; if it is trapped on the tongue it forms a {{c2::lingual thyroid}}.
Severe ankyloglossia can cause {{c1::speech}} problems, and surgery to "untie" the tongue may be needed.
Ankyloglossia can cause {{c1::gingival recession}} in the area of pulling (the {{c2::mandibular anterior lingual}} surfaces).
Initiation stage: the {{c1::oral epithelium}} grows into the ectomesenchyme, forming the {{c2::dental lamina}}.
Bud stage: cells {{c1::condense}} to develop into a {{c2::tooth germ}}.

In the cap stage a 3-part structure appears: the enamel organ → future {{c1::enamel}}; the dental papilla → future {{c2::dentin and pulp}}; the dental sac (follicle) → future {{c3::PDL, cementum, and alveolar bone}}.
In the cap stage, cells begin to {{c1::organize}} but have not yet {{c2::differentiated}}.
In the bell stage (cytodifferentiation begins), the inner enamel epithelium becomes {{c1::ameloblasts}} (→ enamel) and the peripheral dental papilla cells become {{c2::odontoblasts}} (→ dentin).
In the bell stage, dental sac cells begin pre-programming into {{c1::cementoblasts}} (and other cells) for later.
The {{c1::final shape of the crown}} is determined in the {{c2::bell}} stage.
In the apposition stage, {{c1::odontoblasts}} lay down {{c2::predentin}} first; then {{c3::ameloblasts}} lay down enamel on top (moving outward).
cloze.extra: Same rule in the Enamel section: odontoblasts produce predentin before ameloblasts produce enamel.

cloze.text: In the apposition stage, {{c1::cementoblasts}} begin to form cementum at the root surface, and the {{c2::PDL and alveolar bone}} start to form from the dental sac.
Maturation stage: {{c1::mineralization}} of all layers — dentin and enamel calcify with {{c2::hydroxyapatite}}.
In the maturation stage, cementum continues forming and {{c1::PDL fibers}} attach to cementum and bone; the final structures are strengthened and functional.
Dentin forms in bell → apposition → maturation: {{c1::odontoblasts}} from the {{c2::dental papilla}} secrete predentin, which mineralizes into dentin.
Enamel forms in bell (after dentin) → apposition → maturation: ameloblasts from the {{c1::inner enamel epithelium}} lay down enamel matrix {{c2::after dentin}} is formed.
Cementum forms in apposition (root phase) → maturation: {{c1::HERS}} disintegrates → dental sac cells become cementoblasts → secrete {{c2::cementoid}} → mineralize.
The PDL forms in apposition → maturation (the {{c1::eruption}} phase): dental sac cells differentiate into {{c2::fibroblasts}}, which form collagen fibers that insert into cementum and bone.
Alveolar bone: dental sac cells become {{c1::osteoblasts}}, which form bone around the developing root; the bone {{c2::remodels throughout life}} with function.
{{c1::Amelogenesis}} is the production of enamel; {{c2::ameloblasts}} are the cells that form enamel.
{{c1::Tomes' process}} extends from ameloblasts at the DEJ, shaping enamel rods as enamel is laid over dentin.
Once enamel formation is complete, Tomes' process {{c1::disappears}}, and the {{c2::DEJ}} remains as the strong boundary between enamel and dentin.
The outer enamel epithelium is the protective outer layer of the enamel organ; it maintains {{c1::shape and nutrient transfer}}.
After enamel formation, the outer enamel epithelium collapses and fuses with the other layers to form the {{c1::reduced enamel epithelium (REE)}}.
Damage to the outer enamel epithelium may affect enamel mineralization or the {{c1::eruption pathway}}.
The inner enamel epithelium differentiates into ameloblasts, which form enamel from the {{c1::DEJ outward}}.
After eruption the ameloblasts disappear, so enamel has no vital cells and {{c1::cannot be repaired (no regeneration)}}.
Fever, trauma, or genetics can disrupt ameloblasts (inner enamel epithelium), causing {{c1::enamel hypoplasia}} or {{c2::amelogenesis imperfecta}}.
The {{c1::stratum intermedium}} supports and nourishes ameloblasts and is essential for enamel {{c2::mineralization}}.
The stratum intermedium fuses into the REE and is {{c1::lost before eruption}}.
Disruption of the stratum intermedium can impair enamel hardening ({{c1::hypocalcification}}).
The {{c1::stellate reticulum}} cushions and supports the inner layers and maintains {{c2::space and hydration}} for cell function; it also collapses and becomes part of the REE.
Early collapse of the stellate reticulum may reduce enamel {{c1::thickness}} or affect {{c2::rod structure}}.
The basic unit of enamel is the {{c1::enamel rod (prism)}}, which is shaped like a {{c2::fish (head and tail)}}.
Enamel rods (prisms) run from the {{c1::DEJ}} to the {{c2::enamel surface}}.
Once erupted, enamel continues to mineralize through {{c1::fluoride and calcium}} uptake from the oral environment; fluoride creates {{c2::fluorapatite}} from existing hydroxyapatite.
Enamel does not cover the {{c1::root}} surfaces; it is only on the crown.
{{c1::Hunter-Schreger bands}} are light/dark bands perpendicular to the DEJ, caused by the curvature and changing direction of enamel rods and seen in {{c2::reflected light}}.
The {{c1::lines of Retzius}} are dark incremental growth lines in enamel, like rings in a tree, representing rhythmic enamel deposition.
{{c1::Perikymata}} are surface grooves formed by the ends of the Retzius lines (their surface expression).
Perikymata are visible on {{c1::newly erupted}} teeth and fade with {{c2::age and wear}}.
The {{c1::neonatal line}} is a pronounced dark line in enamel (and dentin) formed at birth, reflecting disrupted ameloblast activity due to birth trauma.
{{c1::Enamel spindles}} are short, linear extensions from dentin crossing the DEJ into enamel, caused by trapped {{c2::odontoblast processes}}.
{{c1::Enamel tufts}} are brush-like areas of hypomineralized enamel at the DEJ, caused by abrupt changes in rod orientation; they are {{c2::not pathological}}.
{{c1::Enamel lamellae}} are long cracks or defects running from the enamel surface toward the DEJ, caused by stress, trauma, or incomplete mineralization.
The dental papilla is the {{c1::inner}} part of the tooth germ; the dental sac (dental follicle) is the {{c2::outer}} layer surrounding the tooth germ.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused: the papilla builds the tooth itself (inside stuff); the sac builds the surrounding support system.

cloze.text: Dentin forms the {{c1::bulk}} of the tooth and is present in both the {{c2::crown and root}}.
{{c1::Dentinogenesis}} is the production of dentin; {{c2::odontoblasts}} are the cells that form dentin.
The dental papilla forms the dentin and pulp on the {{c1::concave}} side (the area inside the arch); it is an {{c2::ectomesenchymal}} product.
{{c1::Preameloblasts}} initiate the differentiation of odontoblasts along the DEJ.
Odontoblasts elongate and travel toward the {{c1::pulp}}, depositing {{c2::predentin}}, which eventually calcifies.
Dentinal tubules extend from the {{c1::DEJ}} in the crown, or the {{c2::DCJ (dentinocemental junction)}} in the root, to the outer wall of the pulp.
Unlike enamel, dentin {{c1::stays vital}} throughout the life of the tooth because the odontoblasts' bodies remain alive along the {{c2::outer pulpal wall}}.
Dentin is {{c1::yellow}} in appearance and is {{c2::less}} resistant to wear and acid attacks than enamel.
The {{c1::imbrication lines of von Ebner}} are incremental lines of {{c2::daily}} growth within the dentin.
cloze.extra: Like enamel, dentin shows incremental lines and structural features that reflect its formation and responses to stimuli.

cloze.text: The {{c1::contour line of Owen}} is a prominent line in dentin caused by disturbances in the body that affect odontoblasts during dentin formation.
{{c1::Tomes' granular layer}} is the outer portion of dentin beneath the root cementum, adjacent to the {{c2::DCJ}}.
cloze.extra: Not to be confused with Tomes' process, which forms enamel.

cloze.text: {{c1::Peritubular}} dentin is formed immediately around the odontoblastic process and is {{c2::more}} mineralized.
In peritubular dentin, the tubule diameter {{c1::narrows}} with age due to deposition.
{{c1::Intertubular}} dentin is the {{c2::less}} mineralized dentin that remains in between the tubules.
cloze.extra: The book prints "Intratubular"; the standard term for the dentin between the tubules is intertubular.

cloze.text: {{c1::Mantle}} dentin is the first layer of dentin, next to the DEJ.
{{c1::Circumpulpal}} dentin is the layer of dentin around the outer pulpal wall.
{{c1::Primary}} dentin is formed before completion of the {{c2::apical foramen}} during tooth development.
Primary dentin includes {{c1::mantle and circumpulpal}} dentin and makes up the {{c2::majority}} of the tooth's dentin.
{{c1::Secondary}} dentin forms after root development is complete and continues slowly over life, reducing {{c2::pulp chamber size}} with age.
{{c1::Tertiary (reparative, reactive)}} dentin is formed in response to a {{c2::localized trauma}}.
{{c1::Sclerotic}} dentin is fully calcified dentin associated with {{c2::chronic injury}}.
The root is derived from the {{c1::cervical portion}} of the {{c2::enamel organ}}.
{{c1::Hertwig's epithelial root sheath (HERS)}} is derived from the enamel organ and plays a fundamental role in the formation and shaping of tooth roots.
The root is {{c1::not}} fully formed when the tooth erupts; it continues to form after completion of the {{c2::crown}}.
HERS is formed by the proliferation of the {{c1::inner and outer enamel epithelium}} from the {{c2::cervical loop}} of the enamel organ.
HERS induces the differentiation of {{c1::odontoblasts}} in the dental papilla, leading to root dentin formation and root shaping — an example of {{c2::morphodifferentiation}}.
HERS grows {{c1::downward}}, signaling undifferentiated dental papilla cells to become odontoblasts, which then secrete {{c2::dentin matrix}} for the root.
After inducing dentin formation, HERS typically breaks down; its remnants can persist as the {{c1::epithelial rests of Malassez}} within the {{c2::periodontal ligament}}.
HERS determines the {{c1::number and shape}} of tooth roots (e.g., single, bifurcated, trifurcated).
Incomplete breakdown of HERS can lead to {{c1::enamel pearls}} on the root surface or {{c2::accessory root canals}}.
The {{c1::center}} of the dental papilla becomes the pulp.
The pulp hosts {{c1::nerves, blood vessels, and lymphatics}}, which enter through the {{c2::apical foramen}}.
The pulp provides nutrition for the {{c1::odontoblasts}} that lie on its outer layer.
{{c1::Fibroblasts}} (cells forming the collagen and other connective tissues) are the most common cells in the pulp.
Layers within the pulp, from the outside to the inside: {{c1::odontoblast layer}}, {{c2::cell-free zone}}, {{c3::cell-rich zone}}.
{{c1::Pulp stones (denticles)}} are calcified masses inside the pulp and can be a complication for {{c2::endodontic}} treatment.
After endodontic therapy removes the pulp, the tooth is no longer vital and may {{c1::darken}} and become {{c2::brittle}}.
The pulp becomes {{c1::more mineralized}} with age as secondary dentin is deposited, so patients may note a {{c2::decrease}} in tooth sensitivity.
The dental sac (the area surrounding the enamel organ) is an {{c1::ectomesenchymal}} product.
{{c1::Cementoblasts}} produce cementum, which covers the entire {{c2::root}} (it is not present on the crown).
Cementum can form throughout the life of the tooth; repair of traumatic {{c1::resorption}} involves apposition of cementum by cementoblasts.
Cementum is {{c1::not vascularized}}, and its percentage of inorganic material is similar to {{c2::bone}}.
At the CEJ, cementum {{c1::overlaps}} the enamel in most cases; they can also meet {{c2::end-to-end}}, and less frequently there is a {{c3::gap}} between them.
Exposed dentin (e.g., a gap between cementum and enamel) can cause {{c1::dentinal hypersensitivity}}.

mcq.question: A patient has lost taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but general sensation there is normal. Which nerve is most likely affected?
mcq.explanation: Anterior 2/3: taste by the chorda tympani, general sensation by the lingual nerve (intact here). The glossopharyngeal nerve carries general and taste sensation for the posterior 1/3; the vagus for the posterior-most part.

mcq.question: During which stage of tooth development is the final shape of the crown determined?
mcq.explanation: The bell stage (cytodifferentiation) sets the final crown shape. In the cap stage cells organize but have not yet differentiated; apposition is matrix secretion.

mcq.question: Short, linear structures crossing the DEJ into enamel are seen in a ground section. They are caused by trapped odontoblast processes. What are they?
mcq.explanation: Spindles = trapped odontoblast processes extending from dentin into enamel. Tufts also sit at the DEJ but are brush-like hypomineralized areas from abrupt changes in rod orientation.

mcq.question: A newly erupted tooth with an enamel defect cannot repair itself. Why?
options: A. Odontoblasts stop working after eruption
B. Ameloblasts disappear after eruption, so enamel has no vital cells
C. Fluoride uptake stops after eruption
D. The stratum intermedium persists and blocks repair
mcq.answer: B. Ameloblasts disappear after eruption, so enamel has no vital cells
mcq.explanation: Enamel has no vital cells after eruption, so there is no regeneration. Fluoride and calcium uptake actually continue after eruption (forming fluorapatite), so C is false.

mcq.question: Which incremental lines represent the DAILY growth of dentin?
options: C. Imbrication lines of von Ebner
mcq.answer: C. Imbrication lines of von Ebner
mcq.explanation: Von Ebner lines = daily incremental growth in dentin. Retzius lines (and their surface grooves, perikymata) are in enamel; Owen lines are prominent lines from body disturbances affecting odontoblasts.

mcq.question: Radiographs of a 75-year-old show markedly smaller pulp chambers than at age 30, with no history of caries or trauma. Which dentin is mainly responsible?
mcq.explanation: Secondary dentin forms slowly throughout life after root completion, reducing pulp chamber size with age. Tertiary dentin forms only in response to a localized trauma, which this patient did not have.

mcq.question: During scaling, a small enamel pearl is found on the root surface of a maxillary molar. It most likely resulted from:
options: A. Remnants persisting as epithelial rests of Malassez
B. Incomplete breakdown of Hertwig's epithelial root sheath
C. Early collapse of the stellate reticulum
mcq.answer: B. Incomplete breakdown of Hertwig's epithelial root sheath
mcq.explanation: Incomplete HERS breakdown → enamel pearls or accessory root canals. Epithelial rests of Malassez are the normal HERS remnants in the PDL, not enamel on the root.

mcq.question: Which cell is the most common cell in the dental pulp?
mcq.explanation: Fibroblasts (forming collagen and other connective tissue) are the most common pulp cells. Odontoblasts line only the outer layer of the pulp.
